Week 1 — Graphic Design Software & Foundations

Day 1: Graphic Design Software

A tour of the apps designers use — Photoshop, Illustrator, Photopea, Canva and more.

Tap to flip
Vocabulary

Photoshop — Adobe's industry-standard raster photo-editing software., Illustrator — Adobe's vector-based illustration software., Photopea — A free, browser-based editor compatible with Photoshop files — no install needed., Canva — A beginner-friendly, drag-and-drop design tool for quick social/print graphics., InDesign — Adobe's page-layout software for multi-page documents like magazines and books.

Different software suits different jobs: raster editors for photos, vector tools for logos and scalable art, layout tools for multi-page documents. This class uses Photopea, a free browser-based Photoshop alternative.

Day 2: What is Graphic Design?

The elements and principles that make visual communication actually work.

Tap to flip
Vocabulary

Graphic Design — Visual communication that uses images, typography and layout to convey a message., Typography — The art of arranging type so it is readable and visually appealing., Layout — How elements are arranged and positioned on a page or screen., Balance — How visual weight is distributed across a design., Contrast — Making one element stand out by making it different from the rest.

Good graphic design isn't decoration — it's communication. Every color, font, and placement choice should serve the message you're trying to send.

Week 2 — Photopea, Pixels & Layers

Day 3: Photopea Interface, Pixels & Raster

Tour the Photopea workspace, then learn what pixels and raster images actually are.

Tap to flip
Vocabulary

Workspace — The arrangement of menus, panels and tools you work in., Panels — Dockable windows like Layers, History and Properties., Pixel — The smallest square of colored light that makes up a raster image., Raster — Images made of a grid of pixels — detailed, but not infinitely scalable., Vector — Graphics built from math-based paths — scalable to any size without blurring.

Photopea's layout mirrors Photoshop's, so everything you learn here transfers directly. Knowing pixel vs. raster vs. vector is the foundation every later editing decision builds on.

Day 4: Destructive vs. Non-Destructive Editing & Layers

Why layers matter, and how to edit without ever harming your original image.

Tap to flip
Vocabulary

Layer — Photoshop's building blocks — stacked, independent pieces of an image., Destructive Editing — Editing that permanently changes the original pixels., Non-Destructive Editing — Editing that preserves the original image and can be undone or adjusted later., Group — Organize multiple layers together into one folder., Opacity — Adjust how visible a layer is, from fully hidden to fully shown.

Layers let you edit non-linearly — nothing is permanent until you flatten the file. Always prefer non-destructive techniques so you can change your mind later without starting over.

Week 3 — Background Removal & Compositing (prepares the Week 7 project)

Day 5: Removing Backgrounds

Remove the original background and prepare a clean subject edge for the new composition.

Tap to flip
Vocabulary

Select Subject / Background Remover — Automatically detects and separates the subject from its background., Smudge Tool — Pushes and blends pixels like wet paint — great for softening rough cutout edges., Fringe / White Line — A thin leftover strip of the old background color left behind around a cutout., Defringe / Contract — Shrinks a selection edge inward slightly to remove leftover background pixels., Layer Mask — Hides parts of a layer non-destructively so the cutout stays fully reversible.

Even a clean selection often leaves a faint white line around the edges. Zoom in to 200%+ and use the Smudge Tool (or Defringe/Contract) to blend that line away so the cutout sits seamlessly against its new background.

Day 6: Smudge Tool + Minimum + Gaussian Blur

Use the Smudge Tool to refine edges, Filter → Other → Minimum to remove a white fringe, then place the subject into the world composition and use Gaussian Blur for realistic depth.

Tap to flip
Vocabulary

Background Removal — Separates the main subject cleanly from the original background., Compositing — Moves a cut-out subject into a new image or environment and blends it with the scene., Gaussian Blur — A soft blur that reduces detail and simulates depth or distance., Depth of Field — The visual relationship between foreground, subject and background elements in a composite., Layer Mask — Adjusts the edges and mask of a cut-out so the subject blends naturally into its new environment.

A convincing composite depends on more than a clean cut-out. Match scale, lighting, color and sharpness, then apply Gaussian Blur selectively so distant parts of the scene feel farther away and the subject belongs in the new world.
Week 3 skills: remove the background, place the subject into a new scene, and use Gaussian Blur where needed to create realistic depth. You will use these skills in the Week 7 “Around the World with a Twist” project.

Week 4 — Advanced Portrait Editing

Day 1: Creating a Passport Size Photo

Crop, retouch and format a professional passport-size photo from start to finish.

Tap to flip
Vocabulary

Crop Tool — Trims the canvas down to an exact size and ratio., Passport Size (2x2 in) — The standard 2x2 inch dimension required for most ID and passport photos., Solid Color Fill — Replaces the background with a flat, regulation color — usually plain white., Dodge & Burn — Lightens or darkens areas to even out skin tone and lighting., Resolution (DPI) — Passport photos are typically saved at 300 DPI for sharp, print-quality results.

Passport photos follow strict formatting rules — exact size, plain background, even lighting, natural expression — so precision matters more here than creativity.

Day 2: Transform & Puppet Warp

Practice Transform controls and Puppet Warp to reposition, reshape, and refine portrait elements while keeping the edit flexible.

Tap to flip
Vocabulary

Transform — Changes an object's size, position, rotation, or perspective., Puppet Warp — Pin-based tool for flexible distortion., Control Points — Mesh points used to control a Puppet Warp transformation., Transform Controls — The handles and controls used to resize, rotate, and reposition an object., Non-Destructive Workflow — An editing approach that keeps the original information available for later changes.

Big Ideas

Use Transform for controlled size, position, rotation, and perspective changes. Use Puppet Warp when you need more flexible, pin-based reshaping. Work non-destructively so the portrait can be adjusted again.

PRACTICE DAY

Day 2: Practice — Transform, Puppet Warp & Export

Use the Week 4 skills in an independent practice task and check your file before submitting.

Day 2 Practice Tasks

Week 6 — Face Retouch, Lip Retouch & Dress Change

Day 1: Eyes & Clothing Colour

Make the eyes sharper and more alive, then change the colour of clothing while keeping the folds, highlights and shadows.

Tap to flip
Vocabulary

Iris Texture — The fine pattern of lines and fibres in the coloured part of the eye., Catchlight — The small bright reflection of light in the eyes that makes them look alive., Glass-Eye Look — The fake over-bright result you get from brightening the eyes too much., Select Subject — A tool that automatically selects the main person or object., Color Range — A selection method that picks pixels by colour., Adjustment Layer — A non-destructive layer that changes the look of the layers beneath it., Specular Highlights — The bright shiny spots on fabric that must be rebuilt after a big colour change.

Real eyes have texture, contrast and a small catchlight, but never a glassy glow. A good colour change keeps the original highlights, shadows and fabric detail.
Open this lesson

Day 2: Eyes, Reflections & Teeth

Add realistic reflections to the eyes, whiten teeth naturally, then put it all into one finishing workflow.

Tap to flip
Vocabulary

Environmental Reflection — A reflection of the surroundings, such as a window, that makes eyes look alive., Iris Depth — The sense of dimension in the iris created by light and shadow., Over-Processing — Retouching so much that the person looks artificial., Layer Mask — Hides parts of an adjustment so it only affects the teeth., Warm Tone Removal — Reducing yellow and warm colour from teeth with Hue/Saturation., Selective Brightness — Brightening only the chosen area while keeping natural texture and gloss., Skin Color Grading — Adjusting the colour and tone of skin so it looks even and natural.

Add light only where the light in the photo would fall. Whiten teeth by removing yellow, not by painting them white, and stop before the person looks artificial.

Week 8 — Clone Stamp, Masks & Face Retouching

Day 1: Clone Stamp, Clipping Mask & Adjustment Layer

Remove distractions with the Clone Stamp, limit effects with clipping masks and keep every colour edit editable with adjustment layers.

Tap to flip

Objective: Clean an image and control edits without damaging the original pixels.

  • Create a new empty layer and set the Clone Stamp to sample Current & Below. Hold Alt to pick a clean source, then paint over the distraction.
  • Use a soft, small brush, re-sample often and avoid repeating patterns.
  • Build a Clipping Mask (Alt-click between layers, or Ctrl/Cmd + Alt + G) so an effect only shows inside the layer below.
  • Add Adjustment Layers (Curves, Hue/Saturation, Brightness/Contrast), clip them to one layer and refine with the built-in mask.
Key idea: work on separate layers so every change can be undone or adjusted later.

Day 2: Frequency Separation & Face Retouch

Split a portrait into colour and texture layers, then smooth skin tone without losing natural pores and detail.

Tap to flip

Objective: Retouch a face with Frequency Separation while keeping the skin realistic.

  • Duplicate the photo twice: a Low Frequency layer (colour and tone, Gaussian Blur) and a High Frequency layer (texture, Apply Image / High Pass).
  • Fix uneven tone and blotches on the low layer with a soft brush or Mixer Brush at low opacity.
  • Fix spots and texture on the high layer with the Clone Stamp or Spot Healing Brush.
  • Compare with the original often, and stop before the skin looks plastic.
Practice focus: smooth tone, keep texture, name your layers clearly.

Week 9 — Text Effect & 3D Text

Day 1: Text Effect

Turn plain type into a striking design with layer styles, strokes, gradients and shadows.

Tap to flip

Objective: Create a stylish, readable text effect that stays fully editable.

  • Choose a bold typeface and type your text with the Type Tool.
  • Open Layer Style and combine Stroke, Gradient Overlay, Inner Shadow and Drop Shadow.
  • Add texture or a light glow with a clipped layer and a blend mode such as Overlay or Screen.
  • Organise the effect layers in a group and keep the text editable.
Practice focus: readable type, matching colours and restrained effects.

Day 2: 3D Text

Give your type real depth with extrusion, perspective, lighting and shadow.

Tap to flip

Objective: Build convincing 3D text and match it to the light in the scene.

  • Create the text, then use 3D → New 3D Extrusion from Selected Layer or duplicate layers with small offsets for a classic extrusion.
  • Set the depth, bevel and material, then place the lights so highlights and shadows agree.
  • Add a ground shadow and a soft reflection so the text sits in the scene.
  • Render or rasterize last and save a PSD with named layers.
Practice focus: consistent light direction, clean edges and a believable shadow.

Week 10 — Double Exposure & Practice

Day 1: Double Exposure

Blend a portrait with a landscape or texture so two images tell one story.

Tap to flip

Objective: Combine two images into one clean double-exposure composition.

  • Cut out a clear portrait or silhouette and place it on a light background.
  • Place the second image above it, clip it to the subject and set the blend mode to Screen, Lighten or Multiply.
  • Refine the overlap with a layer mask and a soft black-and-white gradient.
  • Finish with a Gradient Map or Curves adjustment layer to unify colour.
Key idea: keep the face readable and let the second image fill the shape of the subject.
PRACTICE DAY

Day 2: Practice

Use your own photos to repeat Double Exposure, then try the Clone Stamp, Frequency Separation and text tools from the last weeks.

Tap to flip

Objective: Practise independently and test yourself with Check Your Knowledge.

  • Make a second double-exposure with different images and a new colour mood.
  • Add a text effect or 3D title to finish the poster.
  • Open the Practice tab, work through the files, then complete Check Your Knowledge (30 seconds per question).
  • Save the PSD and a final JPG, and write one sentence about what you improved.
Practice focus: repeat, compare with the Read Me, and keep layers organised.

Week 11 — Text on Any Surface with Vanishing Point

Day 1: Text on Any Surface (Vanishing Point)

Apply realistic text on walls, floors, or objects using the Vanishing Point filter.

Tap to flip

Objective: Learn to map and blend text realistically to perspective planes.

  • Open your background image and create a new layer for text.
  • Go to Filter → Vanishing Point and define perspective grids.
  • Paste or drag your text layer into the vanishing point plane.
  • Adjust lighting, opacity, and blending mode (Multiply or Overlay).
PROJECT DAY

Day 2: Refine Vanishing Point Text & 3D Pop-Out Effect

Refine lighting and texture, then create an illusion of objects or text popping out of the frame.

Tap to flip

Objective: Refine realism from Day 1, then combine layer masking and 3D perspective to make subjects break out of the photo boundaries.

  • Use Clone Stamp Tool or Healing Brush to merge edges; match lighting with Curves and Hue/Saturation.
  • Import an image and add a white frame around it using Rectangle Tool.
  • Duplicate the image layer and mask parts that should appear outside the frame; add Drop Shadows for depth.
  • Use 3D Text with Bevel & Emboss to complement the effect.

Final look: your subject or text appears to pop out from the image into real space.

Week 7 — Around the World with a Twist · Individual Project

Individual project instructions, 15-mark rubric, 50 city choices, and submission checklist for Class of 2028.

Individual Project Instructions

Choose one subject and one city from the 50-city list. Take a high-resolution portrait, replace the background with the selected city, retouch the face naturally, and redesign the clothing pattern to reflect that city's visual identity. Your final image should tell a clear individual visual story that merges the subject with the atmosphere of the city.

Individual · 15 Marks

Choose 1 of 50 Cities

This is an individual project. Select one city and build your own visual interpretation.

Submission Format

1. Final Photoshop File (.PSD)

  • Include organized layers: background, subject, clothing, and retouching.
  • Rename layers clearly (e.g., "Clothing Edit", "Face Retouch").
  • Remove hidden or unnecessary layers for file cleanliness.

2. Final Image (.JPG or .PNG)

  • High resolution (minimum 2000 px wide).
  • Export at quality 10 or higher; avoid compression.
  • Filename format: Firstname_Lastname_City_ClassOf2028.jpg

3. Short Creative Reflection (PDF, max 1 page)

  • Title and one-paragraph concept summary.
  • Tools used: Pen Tool, Clone Stamp, Dodge & Burn, Gradient Map, etc.
  • Design choices: color palette, lighting, clothing influence, composition.
  • Include main challenges and lessons learned.

Week 9 — Phone / iPad Mockup Student Project

Design your own mockup inspired by the images below. Let the visuals guide your creativity — focus on composition, lighting, and mood.

Deadline: Follow weekly schedule

Instructions

1. Design a phone or iPad mockup using your own creative composition.
2. Let the carousel images inspire your pose, angle, or scene — don't copy, interpret creatively.
3. Ensure high resolution (≥1080px for phone, ≥2048px for iPad).
4. Use warm accents subtly to enhance mood.
5. Export your file as Firstname_Lastname_PM.jpg.
6. Click "Submit to Class Drive Folder" to upload your final work.

Mockup Note: A mockup is a visual prototype showing your design concept clearly.
Rubric: Composition 40%, Lighting & Mood 30%, Creativity 20%, Resolution & Presentation 10%.

Creating a 3D Mockup and Composition

What: A 3D mockup is a digital visual showing your design applied on a realistic object like a phone, tablet, or poster. It helps visualize how your work looks in real life.

Why: It gives your design depth and realism. 3D mockups make presentations professional, help with perspective accuracy, and make your work more engaging.

When: After completing your main design (photo or layout), use Photoshop or an online tool like Photopea or Smartmockups to place your design inside a 3D frame or screen.

How:

  • Prepare your final image or layout.
  • Use a smart object or mockup template.
  • Insert your design into the mockup layer.
  • Adjust lighting, reflection, and perspective for realism.
  • Align background color or blur to match your theme.
  • Export the final composition as JPG or PNG.

Quick Tips

  • Use light and shadow to create depth.
  • Keep accents subtle but engaging.
  • Ensure clarity and composition.
  • Send your draft for subject-selection feedback.

WEEK 1 Open · Save · Export

Week 1 builds the file-handling habits you need before editing: create or open the correct document, save an editable working file, and export a finished copy in the format your project requires.

01

How to Open

Use File → Open to bring an existing image or Photoshop document into the workspace. You can also open a file from the start screen or drag a supported file into the editor.

  1. Choose the file you actually intend to edit.
  2. Check the image dimensions and resolution before doing detailed work.
  3. Confirm that the document opens with the expected layers or image content.
02

How to Save

Save protects your editable working file. For Photoshop projects, save the working version as a PSD so layers and editability remain available.

  1. Use File → Save As when creating the first named working copy.
  2. Choose a clear filename and a folder you can find again.
  3. Save repeatedly while working so your latest edits are preserved.
03

How to Export

Export creates a delivery copy for a specific use. Use File → Export → Export As when you need a JPG, PNG, or another final image format.

  1. Keep the PSD as the editable master.
  2. Choose the format that matches the destination.
  3. Check dimensions, transparency, quality, and filename before confirming the export.
Week 1 Vocabulary

PSD — An editable Photoshop document that preserves layers and other working information.
Open — Opening an existing file so it becomes the document you can edit.
Save — Writing the current working document to a saved file so the editable work is preserved.
Export — Creating a final-use copy of the design in a selected output format such as JPG or PNG.
Folder — The physical or digital location where the working file is stored.

Quick tip: Think PSD = master working file and export = delivery copy. Do not replace your editable master with a flattened delivery image.

WEEK 2 Destructive vs. Non-Destructive Editing

Week 2 explains what happens when an edit changes the original pixels directly, why that can become difficult to undo later, and how a non-destructive workflow keeps the original information available.

A

Destructive Editing

A destructive edit permanently changes the pixels or content you are working on. If you later need the original detail, you may have to undo many steps or reopen an earlier version.

Example: painting directly on the only copy of a raster layer and then saving over the original can remove information from that working layer.
B

Non-Destructive Editing

A non-destructive workflow keeps the original information available while edits are applied through layers, masks, adjustment layers, smart objects, or other reversible methods.

Goal: make an edit, inspect the result, and still be able to change or remove that edit without rebuilding the entire image.
C

Raster Images & Pixels

A raster image is built from a grid of tiny picture elements called pixels. Each pixel stores color information that contributes to the complete photograph or graphic.

Important: when a raster image is enlarged too far, individual pixels become more visible and the image can lose apparent sharpness.
Week 2 Vocabulary

Destructive Editing — An edit that directly changes original image information or pixels and can be difficult to reverse later.
Non-Destructive Editing — An editing workflow that preserves original information so changes can be adjusted or removed later.
Raster Image — A digital image made from a grid of colored picture elements rather than mathematical paths.
Pixel — A tiny picture element in a raster image that stores color information.
Reversible Workflow — A way of applying an edit while keeping the source information available for later changes.

Why it matters: non-destructive editing gives you more control. You can compare versions, correct mistakes, change your mind, and keep the original image information available.

WEEK 3 Remove · Refine · Place · Blur

Week 3 turns background removal into a complete composition workflow: isolate the subject, clean the edge, remove a white fringe, place the subject into the world scene, and create realistic depth with Gaussian Blur.

01

Removing Backgrounds

Use a selection method that fits the subject, create a clean subject mask or isolated layer, and inspect difficult edges such as hair, fur, and fine clothing details.

02

Smudge Tool

Use the Smudge Tool carefully around fine edges to blend or restore small areas. Keep the brush controlled and avoid smearing important facial or clothing details.

03

Removing the White Fringe

If the old background leaves a bright halo around the subject, refine the edge instead of accepting the visible outline. A white fringe is especially obvious when the subject is placed on a darker or colorful background.

04

Filter → Other → Minimum

With the subject selection or mask targeted, use Filter → Other → Minimum to contract the edge slightly. This can pull the mask inward and help remove a thin white line left by the original background.

05

Place the Subject into the World

Move the cleaned subject into the new world composition. Match scale, position, lighting, color, and perspective so the subject feels like part of the scene rather than a pasted cutout.

06

Gaussian Blur for Realistic Depth

Use Gaussian Blur selectively to create depth of field. Background elements that sit farther from the camera can be softened more than the main subject, helping the composition feel photographic.

Week 3 Vocabulary

Background Removal — The process of isolating a subject from the original background so it can be placed into another composition.
Smudge Tool — A Photoshop tool that blends pixels by dragging color and texture from one area into another.
White Fringe — A visible light-colored outline left around a subject after the old background has been removed.
Minimum — A Photoshop filter found under Filter → Other that contracts an edge by a chosen amount.
Gaussian Blur — A blur filter used to soften image detail and simulate reduced focus or depth of field.
World Composition — The visual arrangement where the isolated subject is integrated into a new scene or environment.
Subject Edge — A controlled layer or selection edge that separates the subject from its previous background.

Pro tip: clean the edge before adding blur. Gaussian Blur should help establish depth in the final scene, not hide a poorly removed background.

WEEK 4 Transform & Puppet Warp

Week 4 Day 2 focuses only on Transform and Puppet Warp. Use these tools to reposition, resize, rotate, reshape, and refine portrait elements while keeping the edit flexible and non-destructive.

01

Transform

Use Transform controls to change an object's size, position, rotation, and perspective. Work carefully with scale and placement so the subject remains believable.

  1. Select the correct layer or object before transforming.
  2. Check proportions and alignment while resizing or repositioning.
  3. Review the result at 100% before committing to the next edit.
02

Puppet Warp

Use Puppet Warp when you need more flexible, pin-based reshaping. Control points let you adjust a pose, clothing area, or selected subject detail with more precision than a simple transform.

  1. Place control points where you need the strongest anchors.
  2. Move only the points needed for the intended change.
  3. Inspect nearby areas for unwanted distortion before finishing.
03

Keep the Edit Flexible

Transform and Puppet Warp work best when the source information remains available. Use layers, smart objects, or other reversible methods when possible so you can refine the result later.

Practice focus: Week 4 Day 2 is only Transform + Puppet Warp. Do not add unrelated techniques to this class practice.
Week 4 Vocabulary

Transform — Changes an object's size, position, rotation, or perspective.
Puppet Warp — A pin-based tool for flexible distortion and reshaping.
Control Points — Mesh points used to control a Puppet Warp transformation.
Transform Controls — The handles and controls used to resize, rotate, and reposition an object.
Non-Destructive Workflow — An editing approach that keeps original information available for later changes.

Week 4 focus: Transform gives you controlled movement and scaling; Puppet Warp gives you flexible reshaping. Practice both deliberately and inspect the surrounding pixels after every major adjustment.

WEEK 5 Revision · Weeks 1–4 Released

Week 5 is a revision week. This note pulls together everything from Weeks 1–4 so you can check your understanding before the skills check: file handling, raster images, non-destructive editing, background removal and blur, then Transform and Puppet Warp. There is no quiz on this note — when you finish, choose Mark as Read and send a short note to your instructor.

W1

Week 1 — Open · Save · Export

Open an existing file with File → Open, save your editable PSD as the master working file, and use File → Export → Export As for a delivery copy such as JPG or PNG. Never replace your editable master with a flattened export.

W2

Week 2 — Destructive vs. Non-Destructive

A destructive edit permanently changes pixels; a non-destructive edit keeps the original available through layers, masks, adjustment layers and smart objects. A raster image is a grid of pixels, so work reversibly whenever you can.

W3

Week 3 — Remove · Refine · Place · Blur

Isolate the subject, use the Smudge Tool carefully on fine edges, remove the white fringe with Filter → Other → Minimum, place the subject in the new scene, then add Gaussian Blur to the background for depth. Clean the edge before adding blur.

W4

Week 4 — Transform & Puppet Warp

Transform controls size, position, rotation and perspective. Puppet Warp uses pins (control points) for flexible reshaping. Keep the edit flexible with layers or smart objects and inspect surrounding pixels after each adjustment.

Revision Vocabulary

PSD — Editable Photoshop master file that keeps layers.

Export — A final-use copy (JPG, PNG) made for delivery.

Non-Destructive Editing — Editing that keeps original information available.

Raster Image / Pixel — An image built from a grid of colored pixels.

White Fringe — Light outline left after background removal; fix with Filter → Other → Minimum.

Gaussian Blur — Blur filter used to soften detail and create depth.

Transform — Changes size, position, rotation or perspective.

Puppet Warp — Pin-based tool for flexible reshaping.

Revision checklist: Can you save a PSD and export a JPG? Can you explain destructive vs. non-destructive? Can you remove a background, clean the white fringe and add depth with Gaussian Blur? Can you use Transform and Puppet Warp without damaging the original? Note anything unsure in your feedback to the instructor.

WEEK 6 Face Retouch, Lip Retouch & Dress Change

Week 6 has two lesson days. Day 1: bring the eyes to life, then change the colour of clothing. Day 2: add realistic reflections to the eyes, whiten teeth, and put the whole finishing workflow together. Work on separate layers so every edit can be undone.

01

Day 1 · Eyes and Reflections (Part 1)

Enhance the eyes naturally by sharpening the iris texture, boosting contrast and softly clearing red veins. Highlight the natural catchlights and brighten dull eyes without creating a fake glass-eye look.

02

Day 1 · Change the Colour of Clothing (Parts 1 and 2)

Isolate the fabric with Select Subject and Color Range, then shift the hue with an adjustment layer while keeping the natural highlights, soft shadows and texture. For difficult changes, such as dark to bright or to pure white or black, rebuild the contrast curves, specular highlights and bounce light by hand.

03

Day 2 · Eyes and Reflections (Part 2)

Add realistic light catchlights and environmental reflections to the irises. Use blending techniques that increase iris depth and dimension without over-processing the eyes.

04

Day 2 · Teeth Whitening and the Finishing Workflow

Isolate the teeth with a precise layer mask, remove yellow and warm tones with Hue/Saturation (warm tone removal) and brighten selectively while keeping the tooth texture and gloss. Then combine eye enhancement, teeth whitening, skin color grading and a global contrast adjustment into one fast, repeatable workflow.

Week 6 Vocabulary

Iris Texture — The fine pattern of lines and fibres in the coloured part of the eye., Catchlight — The small bright reflection of light in the eyes that makes them look alive., Glass-Eye Look — The fake over-bright result you get from brightening the eyes too much., Select Subject — A tool that automatically selects the main person or object., Color Range — A selection method that picks pixels by colour., Adjustment Layer — A non-destructive layer that changes the look of the layers beneath it., Specular Highlights — The bright shiny spots on fabric that must be rebuilt after a big colour change., Environmental Reflection — A reflection of the surroundings, such as a window, that makes eyes look alive., Iris Depth — The sense of dimension in the iris created by light and shadow., Over-Processing — Retouching so much that the person looks artificial., Layer Mask — Hides parts of an adjustment so it only affects the teeth., Warm Tone Removal — Reducing yellow and warm colour from teeth with Hue/Saturation., Selective Brightness — Brightening only the chosen area while keeping natural texture and gloss., Skin Color Grading — Adjusting the colour and tone of skin so it looks even and natural.

Week 6 focus: good retouching is invisible. Make small changes on separate layers, zoom in to check them, then zoom out to see whether the whole picture still looks natural.

WEEK 8 Clone Stamp, Masks & Face Retouching

Week 8 is a lesson week. Day 1 covers the Clone Stamp, clipping masks and adjustment layers. Day 2 covers Frequency Separation and face retouching.

01

Day 1 — Clone Stamp

Create an empty layer, set Sample to Current & Below, hold Alt to choose a clean source and paint with a soft brush. Re-sample often so patterns do not repeat, and zoom to 100% to check the result.

02

Day 1 — Clipping Mask & Adjustment Layer

A clipping mask limits a layer to the shape of the layer below it (Alt-click between layers). Adjustment layers such as Curves or Hue/Saturation change colour without touching pixels; clip them so they affect only one layer and refine them with their mask.

03

Day 2 — Frequency Separation

Split the portrait into a Low Frequency layer (colour and tone) and a High Frequency layer (texture). Smooth tone on the low layer and repair blemishes on the high layer so the skin keeps its natural texture.

04

Day 2 — Face Retouch

Work in small steps, compare with the original, and keep pores, freckles and character. Stop before the face looks plastic. Group and name your layers so the edit stays reversible.

Week 8 Vocabulary

Clone Stamp — A tool that paints pixels copied from another part of the image., Clipping mask — A mask that restricts a layer to the shape of the layer below it., Adjustment layer — A non-destructive layer that changes the look of the layers beneath it., Frequency separation — A retouching method that splits an image into colour/tone and texture layers., Non-destructive editing — A technique that preserves the original image while edits remain adjustable.

WEEK 9 Text Effect & 3D Text

Week 9 develops typography. Day 1 builds a styled text effect with layer styles. Day 2 turns text into convincing 3D text with depth, lighting and shadow.

01

Day 1 — Text Effect

Start with a bold, readable typeface. Combine Stroke, Gradient Overlay, Inner Shadow and Drop Shadow in Layer Style, then add texture or glow with a clipped layer and a blend mode. Keep the text editable and group the effect layers.

02

Day 1 — Colour & Contrast

Choose two or three colours that match the background. Check that the text is readable at small size and avoid stacking too many effects.

03

Day 2 — 3D Text

Create the text, then extrude it with 3D → New 3D Extrusion from Selected Layer, or build a classic extrusion with duplicated layers and small offsets. Set depth, bevel and material.

04

Day 2 — Light & Shadow

Place lights so highlights and shadows agree with the scene, then add a ground shadow and a soft reflection. Render or rasterize last and keep a PSD with named layers.

Week 9 Vocabulary

Layer style — An effect applied to a layer, such as stroke, gradient or shadow., Gradient overlay — A layer style that fills a layer with a blend of colours., 3D extrusion — A visual illusion of depth created by extending the face of text into space., Bevel and emboss — A layer style that adds highlights and shadows to give edges depth., Drop shadow — A soft shadow that makes a layer look lifted off the background.

WEEK 10 Double Exposure & Practice

Week 10 starts with Double Exposure on Day 1 and finishes with a Practice day on Day 2, where you repeat the techniques and test yourself with Check Your Knowledge.

01

Day 1 — Double Exposure

Cut out a clear portrait or silhouette, then place a landscape or texture above it. Clip the second image to the subject and set the blend mode to Screen, Lighten or Multiply.

02

Day 1 — Blend & Refine

Use a layer mask with a soft gradient to control the overlap. Keep the face readable, avoid muddy midtones and unify the colour with a Gradient Map or Curves adjustment layer.

03

Day 2 — Practice

Make a new composition with your own photos, add a text effect or 3D title, and apply the Clone Stamp and Frequency Separation skills from Week 8.

04

Check Your Knowledge

Open the Practice tab and answer the image-based questions one at a time. You have 30 seconds for each question and a review at the end.

Week 10 Vocabulary

Double exposure — A composite in which two or more images are blended into one visual., Clipping mask — A mask that restricts a layer to the shape of the layer below it., Blend mode — A setting that controls how a layer mixes with the layers below it., Layer mask — A grayscale mask that controls where a layer is visible or hidden., Gradient map — An adjustment that maps the tones of an image to a colour gradient.

REFERENCE Additional Portrait & Clothing Techniques

These recordings are released for extra practice. They carry no marks and their pop-out quizzes are for your own revision.

01

Add a Design on a Dress (Parts 1 and 2)

Place your artwork on the dress and use a displacement map so it follows the folds. Then match the lighting, shadows and micro-texture with blend modes, Blend-If and a layer mask so the design looks printed on the cloth.

02

Uneven Eyes: Liquify and Transform (Parts 1 and 2)

Most faces have small asymmetry. Use the Liquify filter and scaling transforms, with guide lines to check eyelid and eyebrow heights, and keep the change subtle. In Part 2, match the lighting direction and shadow density on both eyes.

03

Lip and Face Retouching

Remove blemishes with the Healing Brush, even out skin tone with Frequency Separation and shape the face with Dodge & Burn. For the lips, smooth the texture, balance the colour and add a soft highlight so they look natural, not painted.

04

Puppet Warp: Control Pins and Mesh

Use Puppet Warp to change a pose or smooth clothing wrinkles. Place control pins only where you need them, choose a good mesh density and move one pin at a time with small, gentle moves. This lesson belongs to Week 4.

Additional Vocabulary

Puppet Warp — Reshapes part of an image with a mesh and control pins so it bends without distorting the area around it., Control Pin — A point placed on the Puppet Warp mesh to hold an area still or to bend it., Liquify Filter — A filter that pushes and pulls pixels to gently reshape features such as eyelids and eyebrows., Facial Asymmetry — The small natural differences between the left and right sides of a face., Displacement Map — A greyscale image that makes a design bend with the folds of the fabric., Blend-If — A layer setting that hides or shows pixels by their brightness so a design sits inside the fabric., Micro-Texture — Fine fabric detail that makes a design look printed on the cloth., Healing Brush — A tool that samples nearby pixels and blends them in to remove blemishes., Frequency Separation — Splitting a photo into a colour/tone layer and a texture layer so each can be retouched separately., Dodge & Burn — Lightening (dodge) and darkening (burn) small areas to shape light and shadow.
